boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Fort Sanders record (November 29, 1863) in Longstreet's Knoxville Campaign [November-December 1863]. The simultaneous attack south of the river and the siege from November 17 are outside this record or context. The siege, the November 23–25 actions, the pursuit and campaign-wide figures are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field has unit names only; the live field reads zero. Burnside gives about 12,000 effective men in Knoxville against an enemy estimated at 20,000 to 23,000 including cavalry, and says the assaulting column was three brigades, reinforced by a second column. Longstreet says three of McLaws's brigades made the assault, with Anderson's brigade following, and earlier that the enemy had as many as he did in a strong fortified position.
claims.rationale: Garrison, army and assault-column figures differ in scope; none is adopted. Live zeros are not measured absence.

claims.value: Burnside says the fort was begun by the Confederates before the Federals entered East Tennessee and much improved by Poe's engineers, that abatis, chevaux-de-frise and wire entanglements were made where needed, and that traverses protected the garrison. NPS says the ditch was twelve feet wide and four to ten feet deep with vertical sides. Longstreet says the troops could not pass the ditch for want of ladders.
claims.rationale: The fort, ditch and entanglements existed before the assault; their construction during the preceding siege is a commander decision not credited here. No map verification.

claims.value: Burnside says rations were reduced during the siege, useless animals killed to save forage, and the garrison kept from absolute want. Longstreet says his limited transport had brought no intrenching tools except his pioneers', and that picks and spades captured at Lenoir's were brought up on horseback.
claims.rationale: Supply statements from interested accounts covering the siege, not only the day; no return inspected.

claims.value: Longstreet says rumors of a battle at Chattanooga led him to decide he must attack, and that approaching the fort he saw men straggling back. Burnside says the night advance of Confederate pickets led the defenders to expect an attack there, and that Lieutenant Benjamin roused the men early. NPS says Longstreet believed a storming party could assemble undetected at night.
claims.rationale: Attributed knowledge from interested accounts and a summary.

claims.value: Longstreet says the assaulting lines were formed several hundred yards behind the rifle-pits instead of close up on them. Burnside credits Lieutenant Benjamin and Ferrero's division. The frozen commanders are Lieutenant General Longstreet and Major General Burnside; the live heading ranks Longstreet Major General.
claims.rationale: Judgments are attributed; the frozen commanders do not receive automatic sole credit, and the live rank is not adopted.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Union victory. Longstreet says the column broke up and fell back in confusion; NPS says the attack lasted twenty minutes and calls it the decisive battle of the campaign.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. NPS's 'decisive' is a campaign judgment.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 880 (US 100; CS 780); the live field reads 815 (US 15; CS 800). Burnside reported on November 30 about 300 prisoners, about 500 Confederate killed and wounded, 98 dead passed through his hands and his own loss about 20; his 1865 report says the enemy's loss was certainly over 1,000 and his own 13. Longstreet names three colonels found dead in the ditch.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Burnside's two reports differ from each other.

open_questions: Poe's, Benjamin's, Ferrero's, McLaws's and Alexander's reports, the McLaws court-martial and the returns remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. Burnside's, Parke's and Longstreet's reports, printed in Official Records Series I, Volume XXXI, Part 1, are separate families of interested commanders' accounts; the volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Burnside's full report was written in November 1865 and Longstreet's in January 1864. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
